AnimeAddicts
Video Editing Guide

A reorganized, dark-mode version of the supplied 51-page guide. It preserves the channel’s style rules, numeric settings, visual grammar, pacing logic, examples, reference timestamps, presets, assets, and retention notes without adding outside style rules.

Premiere / AE 2024+ 60 FPS timeline Retention-first Motion > static Source: 51 pages

00 — Non-negotiables

Source pp. 1, 13–17, 19, 29–40, 49–50
60 FPSTimeline + export
1080p1920×1080
15–20 MbpsVideo bitrate
−32 to −35 dBMusic · Normalize All Peaks
1–3 secTarget visual-change cadence
≤3 secStatic-image ceiling
  • Cut all VO dead air. The source repeats this as a hard pacing rule; it also says to remove breaths and chop slow/repetitive narration aggressively.
  • Drop shadow is mandatory on text, panels, PNGs and similar elements. The guide repeatedly reinforces shadows/outlines for separation.
  • Upscale everything: footage and manga panels.
  • Keep assets moving. Avoid static PNGs; use slow pans, bobbing, tilts, drifts, zooms, slides, or a cut to footage.
  • Colored manga panels are preferred. The guide says B&W panels correlated with a retention drop.
  • Intro treatment: motion-graphics/effect heavy for at least ~40 seconds; the first 3–4 minutes should be higher-paced, then gradually slow down.
  • SFX must follow the visuals. The guide’s mental model: an action without its sound feels wrong.
  • Show, don’t dump text. Motion graphics and visual explanations are preferred to text walls.
  • Every shot must justify itself: add information, reinforce emotion, or progress the story.
  • Core retention principle: clarity and cognitive ease outrank flashiness. Control what the viewer sees first, second and third.
The guide’s core aesthetic is a dynamic mix of anime footage, full-screen PNGs/manga, motion graphics, pixel animations, effects, memes and sound — but the later retention section explicitly says the end goal is easy, clear and pleasing processing, not random flash.

Upscaling

  • Footage and panels must be upscaled.
  • Footage upscaling package: source provides a GoFile download and instructs extracting/installing under C:\Program Files\Adobe\Common\Plug-ins\7.0\MediaCore.
  • Manga panels: Upscayl with the Ultrasharp preset is the free option named in the guide.
  • Gigapixel AI is named as a paid option, especially strong for art / CGI enhancement.
  • The source also links a separate UpScaler folder as another option.

02 — Editing identity & pacing

Source pp. 13–14, 26–32, 35–43, 49–50

Primary references

  • Newest primary video — strongest visual target for the channel; use it as the first style benchmark.
  • The 7 Levels Of Cursed Tools in Jujutsu Kaisen — secondary core reference for the 7 Levels visual language.
  • The 7 Levels of Viltrumites — secondary core reference, especially for explainer / ranking structure.
  • What If DIO Was Reborn With His Memories? — reference for animation, PNG motion, power words, data graphics and pacing.
  • Match the reference family in animation style, meme usage, text style, pacing, and white drop-shadow treatment.

Macro pacing

0:00–0:40+
Effects-heavy intro. Motion graphics and visual impact should be dense.
0:00–3/4m
Higher pace. More effects + motion graphics. The source repeatedly calls motion graphics especially important here.
After 3–4m
Gradually slow down. Keep momentum, but reduce the opening-level density.
All video
Alternate media types so the screen does not feel repetitive: footage → motion graphics → full-screen images/panels → smaller PNGs → animations → memes → back to footage.

Micro pacing

  • Add a meaningful visual change every 1–3 seconds as a retention guideline.
  • Never let a single static image sit unchanged for more than ~3 seconds. If narration continues, slow-zoom it or cut to a short anime clip.
  • For non-action shots, the retention notes give a 1–2 second minimum so viewers have time to process.
  • Do not equate fast cutting with good pacing: dense information → longer shot; simple information → shorter shot; tension → slow down; action → speed up.
  • Do not make every shot the same length. Longer shots signal importance; shorter shots can handle simpler beats.
  • Cut setup/build phases aggressively; stretch high-interest scenes properly; do not add filler just to increase length.

03 — Visual mix & composition

Source pp. 1, 11–13, 26–30, 35–42

Default mix

60% footage + motion graphics (including regular motion graphics and pixel animations) / 40% manga panels.

Flow rule

Do not lock into one presentation mode. Cycle between footage, motion graphics, full-screen PNGs, panel layouts, smaller sliding PNGs, animations and memes.

Composition

  • Maximize screen real estate. Empty space without a purpose is treated as lost attention.
  • Negative space is valid when it communicates loneliness, isolation or scale comparison; it is not valid as lazy framing.
  • Crop aggressively when needed. Kill useless space and reframe third-party footage if the composition benefits.
  • Use one clear focal point per frame; avoid clutter and competing points of attention.
  • Visual hierarchy order from the guide: movement → focus/sharpness → contrast/salience → brightness → size → foreground/background position.
  • Important elements should be bigger and readable on both mobile and TV.
  • Zoom for clarity, not merely because zooming looks stylish.
  • Maintain spatial/shot logic. Avoid ‘teleporting’ between actions; add bridging shots where needed.

Visual meaning test

Mute test: play the edit without sound. If a shot does not add information, reinforce emotion, or progress the story, the source says it should be cut.

04 — Manga panels & PNGs

Source pp. 12, 16–28, 30–34
  • Prefer colored manga panels. The guide explicitly says B&W manga correlated with a retention drop.
  • Avoid repeating similar images. Keep the visual pool fresh.
  • Use borders. On dark/black backgrounds use white borders; on grey/white backgrounds use black borders. The guide says ideally all PNGs get some border/edge separation.
  • For story-referencing panels, make the panel large enough to read.
  • One established presentation: panel over a paper/texture background with a thick black frame.
  • Around 40% of the time in the earlier manga guidance, a full-size panel can take over the screen while you pan across or down it.
  • When panning panels: ease keyframes and do not use motion blur.
  • Later flow guidance asks for roughly 50% full-screen PNGs that slowly move up/down/sideways/in/out. Vary the movement direction so it does not become ‘zoom-in only’.
  • For videos that are ~90% manga and have little anime footage, the guide recommends about 60% full-screen panels with slow movement, then other panel presentations for the remainder.
  • Side-by-side panels are encouraged, especially for comparisons. Keep them image-led rather than turning them into giant text walls.
  • Layering is encouraged: one big full-screen PNG as the background, blur it, then place smaller PNGs on top.
  • Piling panels one after another and slowly sliding the pile across screen is explicitly praised.
  • If characters are quoted/talking: use PNG heads + speech bubble + the text as the VO mentions it.
  • If a location is mentioned: a map + simple motion graphics is encouraged.
  • Manga animations from YouTube are allowed and encouraged; memes can be mixed through them.

Do not present a wall of information blindly

  • Only include an image/panel if it adds to what the narration is saying.
  • For a dense page: highlight or zoom the area of importance, darken the other panels, and keep the focal panel at normal brightness.
  • Keep it on screen long enough to actually be read. The guide explicitly says not to flash a wall of information for only ~2 seconds.
  • Avoid big blocks of text; the source associates these with viewer drop-off.

05 — Motion graphics, sprites & simulations

Source pp. 14, 22, 27–34

Pixel animations / sprites

  • Use pixel/sprite animations more heavily in the beginning half, but they can appear throughout.
  • Especially relevant to VS battles and What If videos.
  • When abilities activate, use detailed/moving backgrounds and glow/effect treatments to make the moment feel premium.
  • The source links both sprite-animation references and a tutorial on where to find sprites.
  • The guide later makes simulated fights with pixel animation + motion graphics mandatory for VS battles when appropriate.

Character asset animation

  • Cut character heads into PNGs and give them a slow up/down bob or slight side-to-side drift.
  • Add a 5–10 px white or yellow stroke plus soft drop shadow for a sticker/pop-up feel.
  • Use floating thought bubbles/context icons next to PNG heads when a full clip is unnecessary.
  • For higher-tier characters, a red glow/stroke can visually signify power.
  • Avoid static PNGs: bounce text/PNGs, add slow-moving overlays, tilt then rotate toward center, angle panels, pan, or otherwise keep them alive.

Avoid-static PNG references

Could YOU survive the STEEL BALL RUN race? — 5:43 bouncing text/PNGs, 7:49 paper background + static overlay + slow movement, 12:02 tilted PNG slowly rotating toward center.

The Most Terrifying Stands: The World Over Heaven — 5:13 manga panels angled at 45°.

DIO timing cheat sheet

What If DIO Was Reborn With His Memories?

  • 00:07–00:10 — rapid cut / glitch sequence.
  • 00:22, 00:28, 01:04 — short “Power Word” text hits.
  • 00:34–00:37 + 01:30 — floating character PNG/head motion.
  • 00:54 — thought bubble / context icon.
  • 02:11 + 05:13 — themed data/list graphics.
  • 06:36 — photo/character disintegration effect.

Data graphics

  • Break complex lore, genetics, feats or steps into themed motion-graphic lists instead of VO-only explanation.
  • Chalkboard/UI-style lists can slide or ‘write’ on as the narrator speaks.
  • Build progressively: do not reveal the entire list at once. Add each point when VO reaches it.
  • A Tier Checklist is the named example: requirements appear one by one.
  • Optional: use a power-level bar that fills as levels/topics advance. The source notes this is usually not necessary for every 7-level video.

06 — Typography & on-screen text

Source pp. 11, 18–20, 31–32, 37–39

Primary look

The guide says roughly 80% of text should resemble the shown Montserrat style: big, bold, white, with separation/shadow.

Secondary font

Futura Bold is also explicitly named.

  • Make text big and bold when it needs to pull attention. It does not always need to be huge.
  • For the page-18 examples: use uni.electrify on the green “MONARCH OF PLAGUE” headline. The purple “THE ABYSS” headline is black + small white border + white drop shadow, not Ecto.
  • For a big text beat: blur the background, add the large word/phrase, and support it with SFX.
  • General retention section: text should be used to emphasize, clarify, add context, or support silent viewing.
  • General text best practice in the later notes: white text + subtle drop shadow.
  • Subtitles/text steal a large share of attention according to the guide, so use them intentionally rather than constantly.
  • Text must remain readable on mobile.
Effect ID — do not mix these up
uni.electrify = the green electrified headline treatment in the “MONARCH OF PLAGUE” example.
THE ABYSS = black text + small white border + white drop shadow; the glow comes from the edge/shadow treatment, not Ecto.
Ecto is still part of the AnimeAddicts VFX palette for character PNGs / manga panels and the separate Ecto preset examples.

Typography assets

Font folder / Montserrat pack · Ecto presets

Power Words

  • Short, aggressive kinetic text for emotional beats or transitions.
  • Large bold sans-serif such as Montserrat or Impact, centered for 0.5–1.0 second.
  • Add a small tremor/shake plus a Zoom-In or Pop so the word feels like it hits the screen.
  • Named examples: ELITE, CONQUEROR, APEX during tier transitions.
  • Typing/clicking SFX while text appears is marked as a must-do in the guide.
Context note from the source: the later general retention section says “avoid all caps,” while the Power Word section intentionally uses all-caps single words. Both instructions are preserved here; treat the Power Word treatment as a specific stylized case rather than normal body text.

07 — VFX, overlays & backgrounds

Source pp. 7–12, 16–18, 23–24, 27, 33–34

Core plugin/effect palette

  • Saber (VideoCopilot), Ecto (Red Giant Universe), and Glow on character PNGs / manga panels.
  • Turbulent Displace / Displacement Mapping for wavy, unstable or heat-energy movement.
  • Chromatic Aberration / RGB Split for channel separation and energetic trailing edges.
  • S_Shake for high-frequency camera jitter at transitions or peak impact moments.
  • Scanlines / CRT, VHS / film grain, and halftone as stylistic overlays.
  • Inversion / Negative for occasional impact-frame color flips.
  • Gradient Maps / Duotone for tinting B&W manga.
  • Deep Glow for smooth bloom on highlights/outlines.
  • Film Impact lens, Lens Distortion, and optional Turbulent Displace are named for cinematic colored-panel treatment.

Neon / glowing manga speed-line recipe

  1. Start with speed-line overlays or Sapphire S_Lines.
  2. Use CC Toner / Tritone / Gradient Maps / Colorama to map black/white into deep + neon colors.
  3. Keyframe hue or Colorama for color cycling.
  4. Use S_Zap for jagged lightning or S_Lines for controlled lines.
  5. Add Deep Glow keyed to highlights.
  6. Add Chromatic Aberration for RGB fringe/trails.
  7. Add low-amount, higher-complexity Turbulent Displace to make the lines organic.
  8. Optional: brightness/exposure flicker; the source speculates an expression like wiggle(10, 1) for the referenced look.

Background system

  • Use the provided Glowing_particles_overlay.mp4 and background asset folder.
  • Do not rely only on black + particles. Experiment with solid-color backgrounds, slowed speed lines, and paper backgrounds.
  • Slow the speed-line background so it does not become overwhelming/distracting.
  • The Naruto reference at ~1:14 is called out as a target; the guide suggests turning down the flicker slightly while keeping it visible.
  • Paper backgrounds are good for channel avatars and motion graphics.

Overlay library

  • The guide says the provided Overlays folder MUST be used.
  • Named options include speed-line green-screen backgrounds, VHS/scanlines, moving scanlines, a 35+ overlay pack, blue fire embers, VHS filters and clock/time overlays.
  • In the 35+ overlay pack, the guide specifically calls out: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 11, 13, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24.
  • When time is mentioned, a ticking-clock fly-through or similar clock overlay is explicitly suggested.

Direct VFX / overlay resources

Overlays folder · Speed-line green screen · VHS / scanlines · Moving scanlines · 35+ overlay pack · Rare-character reveal preset

Rare abilities / reveal language

  • Add a question mark to a mysterious character/ability PNG.
  • Silhouette the character in black/white and use two shadows/outlines: black silhouette + glowing white outline, then reveal.
  • For deaths/removal: shatter/particle-dissolve the PNG; use skulls, red tint, or a red X/cross. Pair the effect with SFX.
  • Combat impact: add 1–2 frames of pure white or inverted color on a heavy hit.
  • Optional: slight screen shake triggered by loud SFX or aggressive anime shouts.

08 — Transitions

Source pp. 6–7, 25, 30–32
  • Transition Pack presets explicitly named: both zooms, all spins, push slides (~0:23), stretch slides (~0:32), all swish pans, blur (~0:48), plus other useful editor-added transitions.
  • Mister Horse Premiere Composer is linked as another transition resource.
  • Use Whoosh, Glitch, or Digital Distort when changing characters/ideas; the Jojo reference at 00:07–00:10 is cited for rapid cut/glitch energy.
  • The source uses a rough 6–8 second transition-SFX cadence as a feel reference — explicitly saying not to spam it and not to force the sound exactly every 6–8 seconds.
  • Page-turn SFX is encouraged for manga transitions but should not be overused.
  • Creative zoom-ins/outs and transitions are encouraged when they help the flow.

09 — VO, music & SFX

Source pp. 1–7, 15–16, 29–30, 42–43

Voiceover

  • Remove all silence/dead air and breaths.
  • Remove repetitive dialogue and unnecessary yapping; the source also says to remove something false if you know with certainty that it is false.
  • Maintain engaging narration flow. If the cut feels boring or drags, aggressively compress the slow section.
  • The guide links a Hugging Face silence-removal tool as an option.

Music mix

  • Set music loudness around −32 dB to −35 dB using Normalize All Peaks, referencing the AnimeAddicts Naruto clans video.
  • VO clarity wins. Background music must not distract from narration.
  • Use calm/upbeat music for most standard explanation; switch by the tone of the segment rather than leaving one vibe under everything.

Music selection language

Upbeat / hype

Fight scenes, hype moments, high-energy explanations. The guide also says to use phonk for hype parts and the intro.

Tense cinematic

What-if scenarios, fights, reveals, final showdowns, story-driven tension.

Sad / calm

Use the sad playlists / “Missing You” / “Rain” / the named sad tracks only at emotionally appropriate moments.

Spiritual / ethereal

Use a matching spiritual/ethereal cue when the story moves into a mystical/spiritual idea or realm.

Music theory example from the guide

  • What If Ichigo Was Reborn With All His Memories: around 18:17 the editor switches into cinematic tension.
  • When fighting stops and the scene transitions into a spiritual realm/future-gazing moment, the music changes into an ethereal/spiritual sound.
  • Around 21:17–21:28 the guide stresses that beats and moments must connect.
  • For a slow build toward the reveal of how Yhwach is beaten, the source deliberately chooses a slow tension riser instead of immediate fast tension music.

Named music / source tracks

  • Beneath the Mask (Persona 5)
  • Dreaming
  • Coffee Break
  • Daybreak
  • Chill Upbeat Jazzy Lofi Hip Hop / Jazz-Hop
  • Chill Lofi Hip Hop Beat
  • Rain — only for sad/calm videos or parts
  • future-design-344320.mp3
  • midnight-forest-184304.mp3 — epic cinematic/storytelling, final showdowns or matchups
  • no-copyright-music-hip-hop-379527.mp3
  • no-copyright-music-hip-hop-333685.mp3
  • lofi-song-330550.mp3 — sad moments

Direct audio resources

Anime SFX pack · General SFX pack · Complete music playlist · Premiere VO + music mixing tutorial

SFX

  • Main rule: match SFX to the visual. The source compares missing SFX to a horse walking silently in a movie.
  • Use the provided Anime SFX and General SFX packs.
  • Use paper/page-turn sounds for manga panels, a cinematic hit/thud for impact, data-readout SFX for bar graphics, whoosh/glitch sounds for transitions, and clicking sounds for typed text.
  • The guide’s language is intentionally strong: almost everything should have a fitting SFX, while still warning not to mechanically spam transition sounds.

Final audio pass

Do this only after the VO, music and SFX are final. Make one final balanced version of the whole edit before delivery.

  1. Render the complete timeline audio as one .wav, including VO, music and SFX.
  2. Apply a Hard Limiter at -5 dB. If the result is still too quiet, use -4 dB.
  3. Right-click the final timeline audio and choose Render and Replace with the limited WAV.

10 — VS battle rules

Source pp. 1, 14, 29–30
All normal AnimeAddicts rules still apply. VS battles then shift the visual mix toward explanation clarity and simulated combat.
  • Use roughly 60% footage + motion graphics so viewers have time to listen, process and understand the argument.
  • Avoid excessive text. The guide explicitly says too much on-screen text can overwhelm viewers and make them stop listening.
  • Motion graphics > text explanations when the same idea can be shown visually.
  • Pixel-animation / sprite-based simulated fights are described as a distinctive brand element and later made mandatory when appropriate.
  • Support simulations with effects and motion graphics so the fight feels authored, not pasted.
  • Use high-quality MUGEN gameplay as easy B-roll when a cross-verse matchup exists (example given: Sukuna vs Muzan).
  • Use more transition/editing SFX overall, with the rough ~6–8 second feel reference rather than a rigid timer.

VS-specific references

  • The source links a dedicated VS battle reference as a near-perfect target for footage / motion graphics / panel balance.
  • What If Old Gen Villains Fought the New Gen’s Strongest Heroes? at 1:13–1:20 is specifically called out for simulated pixel fights.
  • Yuji Final VS All Sukuna is linked for additional pacing / fight treatment.
  • Sukuna vs Muzan — The King of Curses vs Demon King is named as MUGEN/gameplay B-roll reference.

11 — Retention, clarity & visual hierarchy

Source pp. 35–43, 49–51

Editor diagnostic checklist

Scene level

  • Does the story move forward?
  • Does it add tension, progress, clarity or conflict?
  • If removed, would retention improve?

Shot level

  • Every shot adds new information.
  • Shots flow logically.
  • No two wasteful shots in a row.
  • Visual progression is clear.

Pacing

  • Compress setup segments.
  • Stretch high-interest scenes properly.
  • No filler added for length.
  • Energy never fully resets to zero.

Retention chart

  • Study slopes, not only percentages.
  • Watch the video while watching the chart.
  • Identify causes of major drops.
  • Do not overinterpret tiny fluctuations.

Clarity rules

  • Prevent viewer confusion at all costs.
  • Remove clutter and competing focal points.
  • Use voiceover or text overlays when context is genuinely missing.
  • Reinforce stakes visually and audibly; highlight risks and possible failure.
  • Use visual cues to show progress, increasing difficulty and stakes.
  • Use structural markers such as progress bars, section indicators and on-screen lists when they help the viewer know where they are.
  • Reinforce the beginning / middle / end of segments.

Continuity & emotion

  • Avoid continuity errors: character/person positions changing without logic, missing reaction shots and broken spatial logic.
  • Always show reactions when they matter.
  • Do not skip emotional beats.
  • Music, SFX and clip timing should make every moment feel like what it is supposed to feel like.

Aesthetic benchmark

  • Do side-by-side competitor comparisons rather than judging a visual in isolation.
  • Rank your result against the strongest channels in the niche.
  • The source states that attractive/clean visuals correlate with willingness to keep watching.

Faces / familiar characters

  • The generic retention notes say faces outperform faceless shots and familiar/main characters usually beat less-relevant faces.
  • Reaction shots matter when they carry the emotional beat.
Meta-rule: the source’s most important retention lesson is that retention comes from how easy, clear and pleasing the video is to process. Framing, pacing, visual clarity, aesthetics and audio all ladder into that.

12 — Script intent, storyboarding & CTA

Source pp. 43–50

Edit the intent, not only the literal words

  • Identify setups, payoffs and rehooks; editing should enhance those moments.
  • Payoffs → bigger visuals. Setups → curiosity visuals.
  • Use pattern interrupts such as zooms, cuts, graphics and sound effects when pacing needs a reset.
  • Show, don’t tell: use visual metaphors, key-line text and motion to carry ideas.

Open-loop structure

  • The source advocates Hook → Deliver → Rehook → Deliver → Rehook instead of one hook followed by information dumping.
  • An open loop is treated as an unresolved curiosity gap; resolve it, then create the next one.
  • The guide estimates the highest-retention ~20% of the script as: hook, open loops, transitions and CTA.

Script handoff / storyboarding

  • Storyboard notes should include visuals, clips, references and timing.
  • Examples in the source: ‘Zoom into face here’, ‘Cut to news clip’, ‘Add text overlay’.
  • The script workflow in the source: idea → angle → hook → open loops → bullets → AI expansion → heavy human edit.
  • Human controls idea, angle and loops; AI can support research, expansion and drafting.
  • Before final VO/edit: read out loud, delete fluff, tighten sentences, add emotion, fix flow; cut repetition, over-explaining and robotic phrasing.

CTA

  • One CTA per moment.
  • CTA types listed: another video, lead magnet, offer.
  • Placement: around the 2–3 minute mark and at the end.
  • CTA formula: Hook → Curiosity → Action.
  • In the edit, use subtle emphasis such as zoom, highlight or a pause before the CTA.

Subscribe + memes

  • Subscribe animation: use one in the first 30–40 seconds and another in the last 30 seconds. Scale, shadow and shake it depending on the scene.
  • Use the MEMES V2 folder and keep some comedy throughout the video.
  • The source explicitly encourages memes alongside manga animations and other visual formats.

14 — Context rules & source tensions

Preserved rather than silently “fixed”

The source evolves across 51 pages, so some percentages and style commands are context-dependent. This section keeps them visible instead of collapsing them into one fake universal rule.

Default compositionEarly rule: ~60% footage + motion graphics/pixel animation, ~40% manga panels.
Full-screen PNG flowLater flow example asks for ~50% full-screen PNGs with slow varied movement.
Manga-heavy videosIf a video is ~90% manga with little anime footage, use ~60% full-screen panels with slow movement, then alternate presentation styles.
VS battlesShift back toward ~60% footage + motion graphics for argument clarity; avoid too much text.
All capsGeneral retention notes say avoid all caps; the Power Word section intentionally uses all-caps kinetic single words for 0.5–1 sec.
“Spam effects” vs clarityPage 17 uses deliberately aggressive language about effects/overlays on panels and footage, while the later retention notes say cognitive ease and clarity matter more than flash. Both are source instructions.
Fast editsThe guide wants frequent visual change, but separately states that fast cuts are not automatically good pacing. Information density and emotional tone determine actual shot length.
SFX density“Almost everything should have a SFX” is paired with a warning not to mechanically spam transition sounds; ~6–8 sec is only a rough pacing reference.
Page-18 text effectsOwner clarification overrides the ambiguous nearby Ecto note for these two screenshots: uni.electrify on “MONARCH OF PLAGUE”; “THE ABYSS” uses border + white drop shadow and no Ecto.
